subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: First Encounters: What Air, Water, and Sunlight Do
periods.activity_description: Students perform the breath-holding exercise from Activity 11.1 to experience air's necessity, then observe a paper firki (Activity 11.2) spinning to sense wind's force. They record observations about air composition, water distribution on Earth, and the Sun's role in photosynthesis in a three-column table.

roles.role_description: Leads the breath-holding exercise, demonstrates the firki, and introduces the three-column observation table.
Perform the breathing activity, observe the firki, and fill in the observation table for air, water, and sunlight.

time_bands.activity: Students hold their breath as long as comfortable and note the sensation; the teacher records responses on the board to draw out why air is indispensable.
The teacher distributes pre-folded paper firki models; students blow on them, observe rotation, and the teacher connects wind movement to windmill function, naming the Indian wind farms.
Students fill a three-column table — Air, Water, Sunlight — listing one observable property or role for each resource using information from the chapter introduction.
A quick whole-class share-out: each student reads one entry aloud; the teacher notes recurring observations to set up the next unit.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening unit anchors the chapter in direct sensory experience before any vocabulary is introduced. Watch for students who conflate 'air' with only oxygen — the firki moment is a good prompt to ask what else moves with the wind. Circulate during the table-filling phase to ensure students are writing observable properties rather than copying definitions.
materials: Pre-folded paper firki (one per student)
Three-column observation table (printed or drawn in notebook)
Blackboard or chart paper for class responses

periods.activity_description: Students carry out Activity 11.4 — collecting or examining pre-brought soil samples from at least two different locations, observing colour and texture with naked eye and magnifying lens, and recording differences in a table. They also examine rock images (slate, laterite, granite, sandstone, marble) and list one property and one use for each.

roles.role_description: Distributes soil samples and magnifying lenses, guides observation prompts, and presents rock images with brief captions.
Observe and compare soil samples, record findings in a table, then examine rock images and note one property and one use per rock type.

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly recaps the previous unit's three-column table, then introduces soil and rocks as two more resources to be observed today.
Groups receive two soil samples (or use samples brought from home), observe colour and texture with the naked eye and magnifying lens, and record findings in a comparison table.
The teacher presents images or labelled drawings of five rock types; groups record one observable property and one named use for each.
Groups share the most surprising difference they noticed between their soil samples; the teacher closes by noting that these observations will help explain why rocks and soil take so long to form.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit continues the observation stage, shifting from air and water to solid resources. A common error is students treating all soil as the same — the two-sample comparison directly challenges that. If magnifying lenses are unavailable, improvise with a transparent water-filled plastic bag pressed flat over the sample.
materials: Two soil samples per group from different locations
Magnifying lenses
Rock images or labelled diagrams (slate, laterite, granite, sandstone, marble)
Observation table (printed or in notebook)

periods.activity_title: Quick to Return or Gone for Good?
periods.activity_description: Students receive a card set listing all eight resources from the chapter (air, water, sunlight, forests, soil, rocks/minerals, petroleum, coal/natural gas) and a clue strip describing how each resource is replenished or not. Working in pairs, students sort cards into two columns — 'renews within a human lifetime' and 'does not renew within a human lifetime' — before the renewable/non-renewable terms are formally introduced.

roles.role_description: Distributes card sets, circulates to ask probing questions, and withholds the vocabulary labels until students have committed to their sorting.
Read clue strips, sort resource cards into two columns, and jot a one-sentence reason for each placement.

time_bands.activity: The teacher recaps the soil and rock observations from the previous unit, then poses the question: 'If all the air in this room disappeared, how long before it returned — seconds, years, or millions of years?'
Students work individually with card sets, reading clue strips and sorting resources into two columns, writing a one-sentence justification for at least four of the eight cards.
The teacher reveals the labels 'renewable' and 'non-renewable' and students check their sorting, correcting placements and updating justifications where needed.

A brief whole-class discussion surfaces contested cards (e.g., water, forests) — the teacher guides students to see that the category depends on whether replenishment is realistic within a human timescale.

periods.teacher_notes: The discovery sequence here is deliberate — students must commit to categories before the vocabulary arrives, so the labels become explanatory rather than merely definitional. Watch for students placing water firmly in the non-renewable column because oceans are salty; this is a productive misconception to unpack using the chapter's description of natural water replenishment. Forests are another useful contested case — the teacher should ask how many years a forest takes to regrow.
materials: Resource card set (one per student: 8 cards)
Clue strips describing replenishment timescales
Two-column sorting sheet

periods.activity_description: Students carry out Activity 11.5 — surveying vehicle fuel types — using a pre-compiled class data sheet. They then map each fuel (petrol, diesel, CNG, coal) back to petroleum or natural gas, classify each as renewable or non-renewable, and explain in writing why fossil fuels are placed in the non-renewable column using formation time as their evidence.

roles.role_description: Provides the compiled vehicle-fuel data sheet and guides students to connect fuel names to their parent resources and formation timescales.
Map fuels to parent resources, classify each as renewable or non-renewable with written justification, and discuss contested cases within the group.

time_bands.activity: The teacher distributes a data sheet showing vehicle types and fuel counts compiled from a neighbourhood survey, connecting to the spirit of Activity 11.5 from the chapter.

Groups map each fuel type on the sheet to its parent natural resource and write a classification (renewable or non-renewable) with a one-sentence justification drawn from the formation-time information in the chapter.
Groups compare their classification tables: where do they agree and disagree? The teacher probes with 'What evidence from the chapter makes you certain this cannot renew in a human lifetime?'

The teacher closes by connecting fossil fuel formation timescales to the broader renewable/non-renewable framework built in the previous unit, reinforcing the criterion of replenishment within a reasonable time.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit deepens the classification work from the previous unit by requiring students to use formation timescale as explicit evidence rather than just category assignment. A frequent error is treating CNG as renewable because it feels 'cleaner' — guide students back to how it forms. The vehicle-survey data sheet grounds the activity in the neighbourhood context the chapter intends without requiring students to go outside during this unit.
materials: Pre-compiled vehicle-fuel data sheet (class survey)
Classification table sheet
Chapter summary reference sheet (fossil fuels section)

periods.stage_label: Explain consequences of resource use and depletion
periods.activity_title: What Happens When a Resource Runs Low?
periods.activity_description: The teacher presents three resource-depletion scenarios drawn from the chapter — dwindling fossil fuels, shrinking forest cover, and unequal freshwater access — explaining the causal chain from overuse to consequence (pollution, habitat loss, shortage) for each. Students annotate a cause-effect diagram for each scenario as the explanation proceeds.

roles.role_description: Presents each depletion scenario with causal explanation, pausing after each chain for students to complete their diagram annotations.
Annotate a three-panel cause-effect diagram, filling in the overuse action, the intermediate effect, and the end consequence for each resource.

time_bands.activity: The teacher recaps the renewable/non-renewable classification from the previous two units and frames today's question: 'Now that we know which resources don't renew quickly, what actually happens when we use them faster than they can return?'
The teacher explains the fossil-fuel depletion chain (overuse → limited supply + smoke + CO₂ → air pollution and scarcity) while students annotate panel one of the cause-effect diagram.

The teacher explains the forest-cover decline chain (large-scale tree felling → habitat loss + soil nutrient loss → ecosystem disruption) and the freshwater-access inequality chain; students annotate panels two and three.
Students compare their completed diagrams with a neighbour and flag any panel where they wrote different consequences; the teacher addresses the two most common divergences aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit shifts from classification to causal explanation — the cognitive step up from Stage 2. Students moving from the previous unit may initially list only 'shortage' as the consequence; push them to name a second-order effect (e.g., pollution, habitat loss) for each scenario. The diagram annotation keeps the didactic delivery active and gives the teacher a quick visual check on whether the causal chain has landed.
materials: Three-panel cause-effect diagram sheet (one per student)
Blackboard for teacher-drawn causal chains

periods.stage_label: Explain consequences of resource use and depletion
periods.activity_title: Water Waste Audit and the Conservation Chain
periods.activity_description: Students revisit Activity 11.3 — examining daily water-use scenarios (hand washing, cooking, gardening) — but this time they construct a consequence chain for each wasteful practice, tracing the action through freshwater depletion to downstream societal impact. They then propose one conservation measure per scenario and explain why it interrupts the chain.

roles.role_description: Provides the activity scenario cards and guides groups to extend their chains beyond the immediate waste to the societal or environmental consequence.
Build consequence chains for each water-waste scenario and write one conservation measure with a causal explanation of how it breaks the chain.

time_bands.activity: The teacher distributes scenario cards (hand washing with tap running, overwatering a garden, cooking water discarded unused) and asks groups to name the first consequence of each wasteful practice.
Groups extend each chain to at least two consequences — immediate (water wasted) and downstream (reduced freshwater availability for others, unequal access) — and record the chain in writing.
Groups select one conservation measure per scenario (e.g., rainwater harvesting, fixing leaks, reusing cooking water) and write a sentence explaining exactly which link in the chain it breaks.
One group shares their chain and conservation explanation for the cooking-water scenario; the class responds with one addition or challenge before the teacher closes the stage.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit applies the consequence-chain thinking from the previous unit to a hands-on scenario, consolidating Stage 3 before moving to evaluation. A common gap is students naming conservation measures without connecting them causally to the chain — insist on the 'why it works' sentence. The rainwater-harvesting example from the chapter (Bawadi, Vav stepwells) is a strong anchor if groups struggle to think beyond 'turn off the tap'.
materials: Water-use scenario cards (three scenarios per group)
Consequence chain template sheet
Chapter reference for rainwater harvesting examples

periods.stage_label: Evaluate conservation choices and judge responsible consumption
periods.activity_title: Judging Conservation Choices: Which Actions Matter Most?
periods.activity_description: Students receive a set of six conservation actions drawn from the chapter (e.g., installing solar panels, cycling instead of driving, practising rainwater harvesting, planting trees during Van Mahotsav, fixing water leaks, reducing single-vehicle use). They evaluate each action by arguing which resource it conserves, whether that resource is renewable or non-renewable, and how significant the impact is — then rank the six actions and defend their top two choices.

roles.role_description: Distributes the action cards, sets the evaluation criteria (resource type, replenishment rate, impact scope), and facilitates the ranking discussion.
Evaluate each conservation action against the three criteria, rank all six actions, and prepare a two-sentence defence of their top-ranked choice.

time_bands.activity: The teacher recaps the consequence chains from the previous two units and introduces the evaluation task: 'Given what we know about which resources renew and which don't, how do we judge which conservation action matters most?'
Groups receive action cards and an evaluation matrix; they fill in resource conserved, renewable or non-renewable status, and a brief impact note for each of the six actions.

Groups rank the six actions from highest to lowest impact and write a two-sentence defence of their top-ranked action that references both the resource's replenishment rate and the consequence chain it interrupts.

Two groups share their top-ranked action and their defence; the class notes where groups agreed or disagreed and the teacher flags that the next unit will use this evaluative thinking on an extended task.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the first unit in the evaluative stage — students are moving from explaining consequences to judging which responses are most effective. Watch for groups ranking actions by personal preference rather than by resource type and replenishment rate; redirect them to their classification work from the second stage. The two-sentence defence is the key product here — it is the bridge to the open assessment task in the following unit.
materials: Six conservation action cards per group
Evaluation matrix sheet (resource, renewable status, impact scope)
Ranking strip

periods.stage_label: Evaluate conservation choices and judge responsible consumption
periods.activity_description: Students work through Activity 11.6 — identifying which natural resources underlie everyday activities (washing clothes, making clay toys, cooking breakfast) — and then write a short evaluative paragraph connecting two everyday choices to their resource impact. The unit closes with the Gandhian quote from the chapter, which students interpret in light of the renewable/non-renewable distinction they have built across the arc.

roles.role_description: Leads Activity 11.6 as a structured class discussion, then frames the paragraph task and closes with the Gandhian quote discussion.
Identify resources underlying daily activities, write an evaluative paragraph on two personal choices, and interpret the Gandhian quote using chapter concepts.

time_bands.activity: The teacher leads Activity 11.6 as a class discussion — calling out daily activities one by one and asking students to name the natural resource (and its renewable status) each depends on, building a class list on the board.

Students individually write a short evaluative paragraph: they choose two daily activities from the list, name the resource each uses, state whether it is renewable or non-renewable, and judge what responsible use would look like for each.

The teacher reads the Gandhian quote aloud and asks: 'Using what you now know about need versus non-renewable resource limits, what does this quote mean in terms of fossil fuels or minerals?' Students write two sentences interpreting the quote.
Two or three students share their quote interpretations; the teacher affirms connections to the chapter's central idea of judicious consumption and closes the arc.

periods.teacher_notes: This closing unit brings the evaluative thread to its natural conclusion by grounding it in personal daily life — the register the chapter itself ends in. A common gap is students writing the paragraph as a list of resources rather than an evaluation of choices; remind them that a judgement requires stating both what they would do differently and why it matters for replenishment. The Gandhian quote discussion is deliberately open — any interpretation that correctly links 'need' to renewable use and 'greed' to non-renewable depletion is valid.
materials: Activity 11.6 discussion prompt list
Lined paper or notebook for evaluative paragraph
Gandhian quote displayed on board or printed slip
homework: Choose one non-renewable resource from the chapter and write three sentences explaining what would happen to a specific daily activity if that resource ran out and why it cannot simply be replaced quickly.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change.

assessment_items.question_text: A student holds her breath and quickly feels discomfort. Which gas in air, making up 21% of the mixture, does her body most immediately need?

options.label: A
options.text: Argon

options.label: B
options.text: Carbon dioxide

options.label: C
options.text: Nitrogen

options.label: D
options.text: Oxygen

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student recalls that nitrogen is the most abundant gas in air (78%) and confuses abundance with biological necessity.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has noted argon from the chapter's gas list but has not distinguished between gases present in air and gases the body requires.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses carbon dioxide — which the body expels — with the gas it needs, a common reversal of the breathing process.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with gas names can approach this by recalling the breath-holding activity: the discomfort is specifically linked to the absence of the gas the chapter names as 21% of air. The percentage clue in the question also provides a scaffold for students who remember proportions better than names.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe at least two observable properties or roles of each of five natural resources (air, water, sunlight, soil, and one rock type) drawn from the chapter, using evidence from direct observation.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Location | Colour observed | Texture (rough/fine/mixed)
Red laterite hillside | Reddish-brown | Rough and gritty
River bank | Pale grey | Fine and smooth
Garden plot | Dark brown | Mixed
assessment_items.question_text: A student collects soil samples from three locations. Refer to the table provided. What does the difference in colour and texture between these samples most directly show?

options.label: A
options.text: Darker soils are always better for growing plants than lighter soils.

options.label: B
options.text: Only one of the soils was formed from rocks; the others formed differently.

options.label: C
options.text: Soils from different places contain different materials.

options.label: D
options.text: The soil nearest to water is always the coarsest in texture.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student holds a misconception that only some soils originate from rock disintegration, not recognising that the chapter presents rock weathering as the universal origin of soil.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student imports an agricultural assumption not supported by the observation activity — the chapter's focus is on difference in composition, not fertility ranking.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student attempts a causal rule from a single data point (river bank texture) and overgeneralises it, reversing the actual relationship suggested by the data.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the table challenging can be directed to compare only the first and third rows — the contrast between reddish-brown rough soil and dark brown mixed soil is the clearest evidence that composition differs by location.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify each natural resource from the chapter as renewable or non-renewable and write a justification that cites replenishment timescale as the deciding criterion.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change.

assessment_items.question_text: Coal was formed over millions of years from ancient plants buried underground. Which statement best explains why coal is classified as a non-renewable resource?

options.label: A
options.text: Coal cannot be replenished within a reasonable time after it is used up.

options.label: B
options.text: Coal is found underground, so humans cannot access enough of it.

options.label: C
options.text: Coal is only found in a few countries, making it scarce by location.

options.label: D
options.text: Coal releases smoke when burned, making it harmful to use.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student conflates physical accessibility with replenishment rate — a confusion between 'hard to get' and 'cannot return once used'.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student uses the harm/pollution consequence as the classification criterion, conflating the consequence of use with the reason for the renewable/non-renewable category.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses geographic distribution (where a resource is found) with replenishment rate (how quickly it returns), both of which relate to scarcity but through different mechanisms.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the abstract timescale concept difficult can be directed to contrast coal's formation description ('millions of years from ancient plants') with water's replenishment through rainfall — the timescale contrast anchors the distinction concretely.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify each natural resource from the chapter as renewable or non-renewable and write a justification that cites replenishment timescale as the deciding criterion.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Resource | Time to replenish after use
Sunlight | Available daily through natural solar cycle
Forest (mature) | Decades to over a century
Petroleum | Millions of years
Mineral ore (iron) | Millions of years
Rainwater | Days to weeks through water cycle
assessment_items.question_text: A student is sorting natural resources for a class activity. Refer to the table provided. Which two resources should go in the 'renewable' column, and what single criterion places them there?

options.label: A
options.text: Forest and sunlight — both are available above ground and do not need to be mined.

options.label: B
options.text: Mineral ore and petroleum — both are found in large quantities deep in the Earth.

options.label: C
options.text: Rainwater and petroleum — both come from natural sources without human intervention.

options.label: D
options.text: Sunlight and rainwater — both replenish within a reasonable time through natural processes.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student uses location (above ground vs. underground) as the classification criterion instead of replenishment timescale — a plausible but incorrect heuristic.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student correctly identifies rainwater but pairs it with petroleum, applying 'natural origin' as the criterion rather than replenishment rate, showing incomplete mastery of the defining feature.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student applies 'found in large quantities' as a proxy for renewability, confusing current abundance with the rate at which a resource returns after use.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the table format challenging can focus on just the 'Time to replenish' column and ask: which entries describe timeframes a living person could experience? That question isolates the two correct answers without requiring the student to hold all five rows simultaneously.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify each natural resource from the chapter as renewable or non-renewable and write a justification that cites replenishment timescale as the deciding criterion.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change.

assessment_items.question_text: A student says: 'Water covers two-thirds of the Earth, so we will never run out of it — it must be renewable.' Is this reasoning correct? Explain your answer using the chapter's definition of renewable resources.
expected_elements: Acknowledges that water is classified as a renewable resource in the chapter.
Identifies that the chapter's definition of renewable is based on replenishment through natural processes within a reasonable time (e.g., rainfall, water cycle) — not on total quantity available.
Points out that most of Earth's water is saline and not usable, so abundance does not automatically mean accessible freshwater is unlimited.
Concludes that the student's reasoning is partially correct (renewable) but uses the wrong criterion (abundance instead of replenishment rate).

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find the written explanation difficult can be invited to answer in two steps: first, write the chapter's definition of renewable, then use it to check the student's claim word by word. This structural scaffold reduces the cognitive load of integrating classification and critique simultaneously.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change.

assessment_items.question_text: Large-scale cutting of trees has been reducing forest cover across India. Which consequence chain correctly follows from this practice, as described in the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: Fewer trees → fallen leaves stop decomposing → soil immediately becomes rocky and infertile.

options.label: B
options.text: Fewer trees → less oxygen produced → the percentage of nitrogen in air increases permanently.

options.label: C
options.text: Fewer trees → loss of habitat for wild animals and birds → reduced biodiversity in the ecosystem.

options.label: D
options.text: Fewer trees → more sunlight reaches the ground → faster soil formation from rocks.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student recognises that sunlight and soil formation are connected elsewhere in the chapter but incorrectly links tree removal to accelerated soil formation — confusing two separate resource processes.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student correctly identifies a change in oxygen production but then makes an inaccurate second step: the chapter does not support the claim that nitrogen percentage permanently increases as a consequence of deforestation.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student correctly recalls that leaf decomposition enriches soil but inverts the consequence chain, treating decomposition as something that stops immediately and soil as turning rocky — a misreading of the chapter's description of gradual soil formation.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle to evaluate multi-step chains can be directed to check each option's first step first ('Fewer trees → ...') against the chapter's forest section, then verify only the surviving step's second link — a two-filter strategy that prevents simultaneous evaluation of all four options.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain consequences of resource use and depletion
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can trace a two-step consequence chain from a specific resource-use practice to its environmental or societal impact and identify one conservation measure that interrupts that chain.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change.

assessment_items.question_text: A family leaves the tap running while brushing teeth and washing vegetables every day. Using the consequence-chain thinking from the chapter, which statement best describes what happens next and what would interrupt it?

options.label: A
options.text: Freshwater is wasted daily → accessible freshwater becomes scarcer for others; fixing leaks and turning off taps when not in use would interrupt this chain.

options.label: B
options.text: Freshwater is wasted daily → saline ocean water gradually becomes drinkable as freshwater levels drop; the chain corrects itself naturally.

options.label: C
options.text: Freshwater is wasted daily → the water cycle speeds up to replace it faster; no conservation measure is needed because water is renewable.

options.label: D
options.text: Freshwater is wasted daily → underground water reserves fill up from rainfall automatically; rainwater harvesting is unnecessary.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student correctly identifies water as renewable but applies renewability to mean 'no action needed', conflating a resource's category with unlimited practical availability — a common but critical misapplication of the renewable concept.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student invents a self-correcting mechanism (saline water becoming drinkable) not supported by the chapter — this reveals a gap in understanding that the chapter explicitly distinguishes between saline and freshwater as separate, not interchangeable, supplies.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student partially recalls the chapter's rainwater harvesting concept but reverses its purpose, concluding that because rainfall refills underground reserves, deliberate harvesting is unnecessary — missing the chapter's emphasis on judicious management.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the multi-part option structure difficult can be guided to evaluate each option in two parts: first, is the consequence described plausible according to the chapter? Second, does the conservation measure named actually interrupt the chain described in the first part? This two-question check prevents students from accepting the first half of an option without evaluating the second.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain consequences of resource use and depletion
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can trace a two-step consequence chain from a specific resource-use practice to its environmental or societal impact and identify one conservation measure that interrupts that chain.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change.

assessment_items.question_text: Burning fossil fuels in vehicles releases smoke and carbon dioxide into the air. Write the two-step consequence chain that follows from this, and name one action from the chapter that would interrupt it.
expected_elements: Step 1 of the chain: Burning fossil fuels releases smoke and carbon dioxide, causing air pollution.
Step 2 of the chain: Large-scale air pollution creates health and environmental problems (contributes to climate change or widespread air quality degradation).
Identifies that fossil fuels exist in limited quantities and burning them faster accelerates depletion as well as pollution.
Names one interrupting action from the chapter: walking, cycling, or using public transport to reduce fossil fuel burning.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to write in chain form can be offered a sentence-frame scaffold: 'When __ happens, the first result is __ . This leads to __ . One action that stops this chain is __ .' The frame does not give away the content but removes the structural barrier for students who understand the concept but find prose organisation difficult.

assessment_items.stage_label: Evaluate conservation choices and judge responsible consumption
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can evaluate two or more conservation actions by arguing which resource each protects, whether that resource is renewable or non-renewable, and what the consequence of not acting would be — demonstrating informed judgement about responsible consumption.

competency.competency_text: Judicious consumption of resources and mitigation of climate change.

assessment_items.question_text: A school decides between two actions: (P) installing solar panels to replace coal-based electricity, and (Q) planting trees during Van Mahotsav. A student argues that action P is more urgent than Q because the resource it conserves cannot replenish. Which reasoning best supports or challenges this argument?

options.label: A
options.text: The student is correct — coal is non-renewable and will not return after use, making its conservation more immediately urgent than conserving forests, which can regrow over decades.

options.label: B
options.text: The student is correct — coal is non-renewable, but action Q is irrelevant because fallen leaves already enrich the soil without human effort.

options.label: C
options.text: The student is incorrect — forests are non-renewable because they take many decades to grow back, making action Q equally urgent to action P.

options.label: D
options.text: The student is incorrect — solar panels use sunlight, which is non-renewable, so action P does not actually conserve a renewable resource.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses the fuel type (coal, which solar panels replace) with the energy source of the panels themselves (sunlight), misclassifying sunlight as non-renewable — a category error that reveals incomplete mastery of Stage 2 classification.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student over-applies 'takes a long time to recover' to forests and reclassifies them as non-renewable, not appreciating that the chapter's criterion is whether replenishment happens within a reasonable human timescale (forests do, eventually) versus millions of years (coal does not).
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student correctly identifies coal's non-renewable status but dismisses forest planting by citing leaf decomposition, which is a separate ecological benefit — this reveals selective recall that underweights the habitat and biodiversity arguments for forest conservation.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find comparative evaluation difficult can be directed to apply the two-question test from the evaluation activity: first, what resource does each action protect? Second, is that resource renewable or non-renewable? Answering these two questions for P and Q before reading the options reduces the cognitive demand of the full comparative judgement.

assessment_items.question_text: Gandhi's quote in the chapter says: 'Earth provides enough to satisfy every man's need but not for every man's greed.' Which interpretation most accurately applies this quote to the chapter's framework of renewable and non-renewable resources?

options.label: A
options.text: The Earth can meet basic needs if resources are used judiciously, but overconsumption depletes non-renewable resources faster than they can form and prevents equitable access for all.

options.label: B
options.text: The Earth produces unlimited resources, and 'greed' simply means taking more than one's personal share without thinking of others, with no reference to resource type.

options.label: C
options.text: The quote means that renewable resources are always sufficient for needs, and only non-renewable resources are affected by greed, so conserving renewable resources is unnecessary.

options.label: D
options.text: The quote means that technology will eventually allow us to create new resources, so greed today is acceptable because future generations will find solutions.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student recognises the social dimension of the quote (sharing) but strips away the resource framework, treating the quote as a moral statement without connecting it to the renewable/non-renewable distinction the chapter builds toward.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student creates an artificial split — renewable resources are safe, only non-renewable ones need conservation — which misapplies the chapter's message that responsible use applies across both categories, especially because even renewable resources like forests and freshwater can be degraded.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student introduces a technological-solution assumption not supported anywhere in the chapter, revealing a tendency to resolve resource dilemmas by appeal to future invention rather than present-day conservation behaviour.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the interpretive task abstract can be asked to match the two halves of the quote ('need' and 'greed') to specific examples from the chapter before reading the options — for instance, which daily activity represents a need and which represents potential overconsumption of a non-renewable resource.

assessment_items.question_text: A village council is deciding between three proposals: (1) install a rainwater harvesting system like a traditional Bawadi stepwell, (2) set up a small wind energy farm similar to those at Muppandal or Jaisalmer, and (3) reduce vehicle use by promoting cycling and walking. Evaluate which two of these proposals are most important for the village to adopt, using the renewable/non-renewable framework and consequence-chain reasoning from the chapter to justify your choice.
look_for: Correctly classifies the resource each proposal addresses: proposal 1 → freshwater (renewable but limited accessible supply); proposal 2 → wind/solar energy replacing fossil fuels (non-renewable); proposal 3 → fossil fuels (non-renewable).
Applies the renewable/non-renewable criterion to argue relative urgency — specifically that proposals addressing non-renewable resources carry greater long-term risk if neglected.
Constructs a consequence chain for at least one unchosen proposal to show what happens if it is not adopted.
Defends two chosen proposals with a named resource, its replenishment status, and the consequence of inaction — not merely listing the proposals.
Demonstrates awareness that both fossil fuel and freshwater issues have societal consequences (equity, pollution, scarcity) as described in the chapter.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find open-ended evaluation difficult can be offered a structured approach: for each proposal, write two sentences — one naming the resource and its renewable status, and one describing what happens if the proposal is not adopted. This two-sentence-per-proposal structure generates the minimum content for a justified evaluation without requiring the student to construct the argument form independently.

assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. For each daily activity: (1) name the natural resource(s) it uses, (2) classify each resource as renewable or non-renewable, (3) describe one consequence if that resource runs out or is overused, and (4) propose a responsible action that reduces its depletion. Then, in two sentences below the table, evaluate which single activity on this list most urgently needs a behaviour change and explain why, using the chapter's framework of replenishment rate and consequence severity.
assessment_items.scaffold: Use the chapter's resource descriptions and renewable/non-renewable definitions to fill in the table. For the consequence column, think about what the chapter says happens when that resource is overused or depleted. For the evaluation sentences, consider: which resource is hardest to get back once it is gone, and what does the chapter say about the societal impact of losing access to it?
format_of_output: Completed five-row table with all four columns filled for each activity
Two evaluative sentences below the table naming the most urgent activity, the resource involved, its replenishment status, and the consequence of inaction

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification or sorting task with justification
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The final stage implied LO requires students to evaluate conservation actions by classifying resources and tracing consequences — a classification-with-justification task directly operationalises this by requiring both the category assignment and the evaluative reasoning in a single integrated product.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can synthesise the entire chapter's progression: identify resources from daily activities, apply the renewable/non-renewable classification with correct replenishment reasoning, construct consequence chains, propose conservation actions, and make a comparative evaluative judgement about urgency — the full cognitive operation named in the dissolution test.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold directs students back to the chapter's own language for the consequence and replenishment reasoning, preventing students from inventing consequences not grounded in the chapter. The two evaluative sentences are the evaluative apex of the task — a weak response will simply repeat a table row; a strong response will argue across rows using replenishment rate and consequence severity as comparative criteria.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses: classify all five resources correctly with replenishment justification, write consequences that name a second-order societal or environmental impact (not just 'we won't have it'), propose actions tied specifically to the resource's replenishment gap, and write evaluative sentences that compare across activities using replenishment rate and consequence severity as explicit criteria. Weak responses: leave cells blank or write vague entries ('it will be bad'), classify resources without justification, repeat the same conservation action for all rows, or write evaluative sentences that merely restate a table entry without a comparative argument.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find the five-row table overwhelming can be invited to complete three rows of their choice first and return to the remaining two — this reduces the initial cognitive load while preserving the evaluative sentence requirement. Students who find written evaluation difficult can be offered a sentence starter: 'The activity that most urgently needs a behaviour change is __ because the resource it uses is __ , which cannot return for __ , and if it runs out, __ .'
